summary:
vostok_hotspot builds one consistent fire-activity record from NASA FIRMS MODIS (2000 on, 1 km) and VIIRS (2012 on, 375 m) hotspots. Merged raw, the two sensors create an artificial jump in 2012, because VIIRS detects about 4–6 times more hotspots in our data. We count hotspots per H3 cell and month, fit the VIIRS/MODIS ratio k per region and season on the 2012–2016 overlap, and rescale MODIS counts before 2012 with 90% uncertainty bands. Known MODIS data gaps are flagged, and persistent heat sources can be excluded. A hold-out test on unseen years gives annual-sum errors of −5% (Tajikistan) and −9.5% (United States). The web app lets emergency managers draw an area, view a burning calendar, compare any month with its historical median and download raw hotspots as CSV.

https://github.com/Jasurios/VostokHotspot
details:
What it does: the app turns two incompatible satellite records into one burning-activity calendar for any area. Users draw a rectangle or polygon on a map, choose dates, and get a month-by-year calendar (accessible viridis scale), a comparison of any month with its historical median, and a CSV download of raw hotspots.

How it works: hotspots are counted per H3 cell and month for each sensor. The ratio k = VIIRS/MODIS is fitted per coarse region and season on the 2012–2016 overlap and applied to MODIS counts before 2012 (counts are rescaled, never single points). Each pre-2012 month carries a 90% Poisson uncertainty interval. Documented MODIS data gaps are flagged and never treated as zero fire. An optional filter removes persistent heat sources (industry, flares).

Validation: k fitted on 2012–2014 and tested on 2015–2018 gives annual-sum errors of −5.0% (Tajikistan) and −9.5% (United States), monthly correlation 0.72 and 0.99. Our first attempt flipped the 2012 jump instead of removing it; a hold-out test then exposed that k drifts over time, so k is fitted on the earliest overlap. Remaining period differences (+4% to +17%) may be real change or residual bias, and we say so.

Tools: Python (pandas, H3, matplotlib) for harmonization; Go, DuckDB and Parquet for the backend; Leaflet and Leaflet.draw for the map. Adding a region takes four steps (see README).

Impact: early warning teams, scientists and land managers get a consistent history without having to know which sensor saw what, and can compare current burning with the historical median.

Limitations: pre-2012 monthly values are estimates; a hotspot is not a fire; small areas give unstable values; not intended for tactical decisions.

Use of AI: code, documentation and slides were developed with AI assistance (Claude / Claude Code). All results were run and checked by the team.

https://github.com/Jasurios/VostokHotspot
